points.en: Scripture begins with sex as God's good gift, honorable and undefiled within marriage (Hebrews 13:4), before any prohibition.
The Christian sexual ethic protects a good thing rather than suppressing it, like a fire kept in the hearth where it warms rather than burns.
Sexual union is ordered to the covenant of marriage between a man and a woman: one flesh (Genesis 2:24); teaching it positively shows its beauty.
Pornography trains the heart to consume image-bearers as objects for one's own use, the opposite of love, which gives itself for another.
Matthew 5:28: looking at someone to lust is already adultery in the heart, so it is not a harmless private matter.
Like enslaving sins it demands more for less, isolates, feeds on secrecy, and corrodes the capacity for real intimacy.
First, confession that brings the sin into the light by telling a trusted brother (James 5:16), which breaks the power of secrecy and shame.
Ongoing honest accountability to others who may ask hard questions, not a one-time confession.
Freedom comes from the grace of God working through the gospel in a person no longer fighting alone, not from willpower.
Study the relevant biblical texts carefully and understand how faithful Christians and their traditions interpret them.
Teach within the ministry setting with theological integrity, humility, truthfulness and compassion, treating everyone as an image-bearer, never with contempt.
CTS does not require adopting one position on disputed secondary questions, and differing interpreters have not abandoned biblical authority.
Divorce was once treated as nearly unpardonable, leaving divorced believers with a weight of shame the church did not carry for its own faults, yet it is now rarely singled out.
So a pastor should not treat any one sin as a class by itself, or build preaching or shame around one sin, since Scripture's sin lists are plural and unranked.
No sin or struggle puts a person beyond grace; a sin God hates and Christ names adultery has been received into the church's forgiven life.
Silence is not neutrality: if the church is silent, the culture will disciple people in their sexuality.
Teaching only prohibitions makes people think Christianity is against sex; showing God's design makes the prohibitions a fence around a garden.
Sexual discipleship happens or fails in the local church.
Never truth without love, and never a love that abandons truth; the two are partners, not rivals.
Christ with the woman caught in sin neither lowered the standard nor crushed her; the pastor holds the biblical design while extending lifting grace.
No one who comes through the church doors is beyond the reach of the gospel.
No sexual sin is beyond the cleansing blood of Christ, and no sexual brokenness beyond His grace to redeem.
He must name sexual sin honestly as sin and call to repentance, never winking at it as harmless.
He must not crush the struggler as hopeless, but walk patiently beside him, holding out real freedom in Christ.
He brings the sin out of secrecy through confession and accountability, relying on God's grace rather than willpower.
Teaching only prohibitions leads people to conclude Christianity is against sex, leaving them defenseless when the culture offers a seemingly more generous vision.
Shown the beauty and meaning of God's design (covenant, the body as the Lord's, marriage as Christ and church, honorable singleness), the prohibitions read as a fence around a garden.
Teaching the design positively protects the gift, since a people who have seen its beauty are better armed against its counterfeits.
